common_name: Service Viburnum (Glossy Evergreen Parent of Burkwood and Pragense Hybrids)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; service viburnum is grown today mainly as historic breeding stock, so full sun gives the densest, most compact habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it where the glossy, leathery, dark-green foliage and silvery leaf undersides can be appreciated up close, since this Chinese species is grown today more often as breeding stock than as a garden specimen in its own right. Rounded clusters of fragrant white flowers 2 to 3 inches across open in mid to late spring, followed by small blue-black fruit that sets more heavily when a second, genetically distinct plant grows nearby for cross-pollination. Service viburnum is the parent species behind several widely planted hybrids prized for glossy foliage and improved heat tolerance, including Burkwood viburnum, Chesapeake, and Pragense, and it passes its semi-evergreen habit and broad soil adaptability on to its offspring. Give it full sun for the tightest, most compact form, since shaded plants grow looser and more open, and prune only lightly right after flowering to remove crossing or awkward growth.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Viburnum utile (Service Viburnum)
Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

common_name: Bitchiu Viburnum (Fragrant Japanese Parent of Judd Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container stock in early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; prune only right after flowering, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving this looser-growing Japanese species more room than its tidy hybrid offspring Judd viburnum typically needs. Bitchiu viburnum, named for the historical Bitchu province of Japan, opens rose-pink buds to intensely fragrant, pale pink to white flower clusters in early spring, a scent reminiscent of Korean spice viburnum but carried on a more open, spreading framework. Small fruits ripen from red to black over summer, though the fragrant spring bloom rather than fruit display is the plant's main draw. It was crossed with Viburnum carlesii at the Arnold Arboretum to create the more compact, disease-resistant Judd viburnum, and gardeners who want the parent's larger scale and looser habit still seek out the species itself. Prune only right after flowering to remove crossing or awkward stems, since next year's flowers form on the current season's growth.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden — Plant Finder: Viburnum bitchiuense

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lisarose, sold under the trademark Shades of Pink, is a patented laurustinus selection valued for flower buds that open through a sequence of pink tones rather than straight to white.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, working compost into the planting hole to give the dense root system a strong start. Lisarose, marketed as Shades of Pink laurustinus, opens deep pink buds that fade through blush pink before finishing white, so a single flower cluster often shows several tones at once from midwinter into spring, a more layered color display than the plain white bloom of most Viburnum tinus selections. Small blue-black fruits follow the flowers and add cool-season interest for birds. Its dense, rounded, glossy-leaved habit needs little pruning beyond an occasional trim right after flowering to remove wayward branches and keep the plant tidy for hedge, foundation, or specimen use.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Viburnum tinus 'Lisarose'

common_name: Cambridge Blue Gentian Sage (Pale Sky-Blue Salvia patens)

planting.note: Plant tubers, divisions, or container-grown starts in full sun to partial shade after the last frost date; named color forms like Cambridge Blue do not come true from seed and are propagated vegetatively.

directions: Plant tubers or container-grown starts in full sun to partial shade after the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Cambridge Blue is a paler, softer-toned form of gentian sage, replacing the species' saturated cobalt-blue with a clear, powdery sky-blue that reads as gentler and more luminous in the border, especially against silver or white companions. Like the species it develops tuberous roots and produces slender spikes of large, two-lipped flowers continuously from summer into fall, drawing bees and hummingbirds throughout the display. Because named color forms do not come true from seed, propagate by division or stem cuttings rather than seed to keep the pale blue color true; lift and store tubers over winter in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily where it is reliably perennial.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Salvia patens 'Cambridge Blue'
Beth Chatto's Plants & Gardens — Salvia patens 'Cambridge Blue'

common_name: Raspberry Royal Autumn Sage (Deep Raspberry-Red Salvia greggii Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; give it excellent drainage, since it is somewhat more cold-sensitive than the hardiest Salvia greggii selections.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, giving this compact autumn sage sharp drainage since it is somewhat more cold-sensitive than tougher selections such as Furman's Red. Raspberry Royal bears small, deep raspberry-red, two-lipped flowers set off by dark, ribbed crimson calyces, a richly saturated color produced almost continuously from spring through fall on a tidy, well-branched subshrub. Its smaller stature compared to many autumn sage cultivars suits the front of a border, a low informal hedge, or a large container, and it draws hummingbirds and bees steadily throughout its long bloom season. Shear lightly after each flush of bloom and give it a harder cutback in late winter to keep growth dense and floriferous.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Salvia greggii 'Raspberry Royal'
Plant Delights Nursery — Salvia greggii 'Raspberry Royale'

common_name: Cold Hardy Pink Autumn Sage (Zone 5-Hardy Salvia greggii Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Cold Hardy Pink was selected in northern Texas specifically for reliable overwintering as far north as zone 5.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Cold Hardy Pink was selected in northern Texas specifically for the ability to survive winters far colder than typical Salvia greggii cultivars tolerate, making it a rare autumn sage option for gardeners well north of the usual zone 7-8 range. It bears creamy-pink flowers cupped by deep red bracts and calyces, a soft two-tone effect, blooming from late spring through fall on a compact, rounded subshrub that stays under 2 feet tall and wide. Like other autumn sage selections it is highly drought-tolerant once established and a dependable hummingbird and bee plant through its long bloom season. Cut back hard in late winter or early spring to remove old wood and encourage the densest new growth and heaviest flowering.
sources: High Country Gardens — Salvia greggii 'Cold Hardy Pink'
FBTS (Flowers by the Sea) — Salvia greggii 'Cold Hardy Pink'

common_name: Bethellii Roseleaf Sage (Large Cerise-Pink Fall-Blooming Salvia)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; give it a warm, sheltered site, since it flowers so late that an early hard freeze can cut the display short.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in full sun to light afternoon shade in fertile, well-drained soil, giving this large Mexican salvia room to grow into a substantial clump by late summer. Bethellii is the most widely grown selection of rosy-leaf sage, prized for oversized, velvety, cerise-pink tubular flowers held in inflated, contrastingly colored calyces that give each bloom cluster an almost peony-like fullness unlike the smaller flowers of most salvias. It flowers very late in the season, from September into November, making it one of the best sources of fresh nectar for hummingbirds still moving through in fall. Because a hard freeze can cut the display short, site it in a warm, sheltered spot at the cooler edge of its range, and cut the frost-killed top growth back to the base in late winter, mulching well where winters dip toward the bottom of zone 9.

common_name: Haematodes Meadow Sage (Large-Flowered Lavender-Blue Salvia pratensis)

planting.note: Sow seed or plant divisions in early spring or fall directly in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Haematodes flowers more prolifically in lean, dry soil than in rich, moist ground.

directions: Sow in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Haematodes is a robust selection of meadow clary bred for unusually large, clear lavender-blue flowers on branching sprays taller than the typical species, rising above handsome, broadly oval, wrinkled basal foliage. It flowers over a long stretch from early to late summer and, like the species, self-sows readily to form lasting colonies in a meadow, prairie, or gravel garden setting. The oversized flowers make it a particularly strong choice where scale and visibility matter in a naturalistic planting, and it is just as attractive to bumblebees and other long-tongued pollinators as the straight species. Grow it in lean, dry, alkaline soil for the strongest flowering and the least risk of the crown rotting over a wet winter.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Salvia pratensis Haematodes Group
